sources.title: The abc conjecture is true almost always
sources.enterprise_use: Records an elementary exposition of the classical de Bruijn estimate and its consequence that at most O(N^(2/3)) coprime additive triples in [1,N]^3 can violate rad(abc)>=c^(1-epsilon). P025 Stage 62 uses this only to audit and bound the novelty/competitiveness of its paired-residual sparse-failure route.
sources.not_claimed: The de Bruijn radical-counting estimate, the classical almost-all abc consequence, and the O(N^(2/3)) benchmark are external prior mathematics and are not Enterprise Math inventions.

sources.title: Bounds on the exceptional set in the abc conjecture
sources.enterprise_use: The current 2026 arXiv version explicitly records de Bruijn's radical-count O_epsilon(x^(lambda+epsilon)), derives the classical N_lambda(X)=O_epsilon(X^(2lambda/3+epsilon)) bound, and gives substantially stronger modern exceptional-set estimates. P025 uses this as the direct prior-art ceiling for Stage 61-64 counting claims.
sources.not_claimed: The de Bruijn estimate, the pair-radical selector bound, the anatomic decomposition, Fourier/geometry-of-numbers methods, and the modern exceptional-set exponents are external number theory and are not Enterprise Math inventions.

sources.title: Arithmetic Subderivatives and Leibniz-Additive Functions
sources.enterprise_use: Identifies the standard arithmetic derivative D(n) with D(p)=1 and the Leibniz rule, records D(n)=n*sum_p v_p(n)/p, and recalls classical upper/lower bounds in terms of Omega(n). P025 Stage 66 uses this to identify its raw derivative mass U(n) exactly with the standard arithmetic derivative and to bound novelty of the orientation selector.
sources.not_claimed: The arithmetic derivative, its logarithmic formula, Leibniz rule, and classical size bounds are established prior mathematics and are not Enterprise Math inventions.
